blocks.h: A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
I began this book from a small question, which is whether a grudge is a burden or an instrument.

We are taught to put down our resentments. Forgive, release, move on, be light. It is offered as hygiene, and mostly it is meant kindly. But a grudge is also a form of memory — arguably the most durable one we have. It is the body's refusal to file something away as settled. Long after the mind has agreed to be reasonable, the resentment sits there in the chest, keeping the account open. It is stubborn, it is unattractive, and it is very often correct.

So I wanted to build a town that had solved the problem. Not a dystopia — Halloran is a nice place, and I want the reader to feel that it is a nice place — but a community that had found a hygienic, administrative, entirely voluntary way to stop holding on. And then I wanted to ask what such a people would be unable to see.

The rest followed from a second question, which is what it costs to be the one who holds it instead, and whether that person is a servant, a drain, or a weapon. In the end I think she is all three, and I do not think the town could tell you which.

There is one further thing under this, which is older than the book and which I will name only briefly. In the tradition I grew up hearing about, the world is understood as a contest between asha — the true order, the way things actually are — and druj, the Lie. What is unusual about that framing is that the Lie is not primarily a false statement. It is a disorder. It is the world made unrecognisable to the people living in it. I have never found a better description of what a certain kind of comfort does.

I should say plainly that there is no supernatural machinery in this book beyond the one impossible thing at its centre, and even that one I have tried to render as paperwork. The horror of Halloran is not that it is haunted. It is that it has a filing cabinet, an order form for ledgers, and a very kind woman who administers the whole arrangement and has never once lied to anybody.
— Chew Z
VERSE THE FORTY-NINTH
Read aloud in the Tithe hall before the taking of each season.
Come with the year still sour in your mouth,
come with the fence line and the debt unpaid,
come with the brother who was given the house,
come with the vow you kept and now regret you made.
Set it down here. The town was never made to hold.
The town was made to walk out light and clean.
What the mouth lets go is weather, and goes cold;
what the hand sets down is carried, and unseen.
So drink, and let the ledger take your part,
and leave here gentler than you came within,
and love your neighbour with a lightened heart,
and never count the cost of loving him.
We do not ask our own to bear the weight.
We send away. A stranger comes by post —
kinless, patient, schooled in swallowing late,
and we call her ours the way we call it frost.
Blessed the town that carries not a stone.
Blessed the ground that answers to one name.
Blessed the closing year that leaves us clean.
Blessed the hand that bears away our shame.
Drink, and be opened. Write, and be filled.
Come to the ending of your carrying,
and we will walk you out at dusk, and still
your hands, and give you a small good house,
and thank you,
and begin.
PART ONE
THE HAND
The bus put me down at the crossroads a little after four and did not wait to see whether anyone met me.

There was a bench. There was a shelter with three sides and a roof of corrugated tin gone the colour of weak tea. There was a road that ran west into the town and east into a field that had been ploughed and left, and there was a sign, white on green, that said HALLORAN and under that, in smaller letters, the population, which had been painted over twice and corrected twice and now read four thousand one hundred and six.

I sat with my case on my knees for eleven minutes. I remember counting them, because counting is a thing I do instead of worrying, and because there was nothing else in that landscape to attend to. The field had been turned over and nothing put in it. There was a line of poplars at the far edge, planted in a row so straight it looked like something a person had done in anger.
Then a man came out of town on a bicycle, and slowed as he passed, and said, "You'll be for the Office."
"I will."

"They'll have forgotten you," he said, not unkindly. "They do that. It's not meanness." And he stood on the pedals and went on east into the field road, and that was the first person I met in Halloran, and he was entirely pleasant, and I want to be clear about that from the start. Everyone was pleasant. That is not a thing I am being ironic about. It is the whole of what I have to report.

I walked in. It took twenty minutes, and the town assembled itself around me the way small towns do — first the outbuildings, the equipment yard, a garage with two pumps and a dog asleep between them; then houses, set back, painted; then a school, which was a low brick building with a name over the door.
The name over the door was STORR.

I noticed it the way you notice a name over a door, which is to say I did not notice it at all, and I record it here only because I have since gone back through everything I saw that first afternoon looking for the moment I could have understood, and this is the earliest candidate. A name over a door. A perfectly ordinary thing. A town has a family in it who gave money for a school, and the school carries the family's name, and nobody thinks about it twice, and that is how it is supposed to work.
The Tithe Office was on the square between the assessor and a shop that sold wool.

I had expected — I am not sure what I had expected. Something with a certain weight to it. What I got was a door with frosted glass and gold lettering, and behind the door a room with a counter, and behind the counter a woman of about sixty in a cardigan the colour of oatmeal, who looked up and said, "Oh, Ruth," as though we had known each other for years and she had been waiting all afternoon.
"Mrs Storr."

"Adele. Nobody's called me Mrs Storr since my mother-in-law died and I don't miss either of them." She came round the counter. She took my case out of my hand before I could stop her, which is a thing people do to you when they have decided you are theirs. "You walked. God, you walked. Nobody told you Terrence would come out for you?"
"A man on a bicycle said you'd have forgotten me."
"That'll be Terrence," she said, delighted, "and he's quite right, and I'm mortified, and you'll have a cup of tea before you see anything."

I should stop here and give the reader the words, because Halloran uses three of them and uses them the way other towns use rates and refuse day, and I had all three explained to me over that first pot of tea.

The Tithe is the collection itself. A tithe, in the old sense, is a tenth — the portion of a harvest a household owes and hands over, every year, as a matter of course. Halloran kept the word and changed the crop. What is collected four times a year in the hall is not grain and not money. It is grievance: every complaint, resentment and grudge a person has accumulated since the last collection, spoken aloud across a desk and handed in like anything else that is owed.
The tithers are everyone who comes to pay — which is to say, the town. Four thousand people, in alphabetical order, four seasons a year.

And the Taker is the one who receives. One officer, always brought in from outside, who sits on the far side of the desk, writes each grievance down in longhand, and — this is the whole of the arrangement, and nobody in Halloran finds it strange, because nothing you have done since childhood is strange — carries what she writes. Not in the book. In herself. The tither goes out the door lighter. The Taker keeps it.
That was the post I had answered an advertisement for. I want to set down what the Office was, physically, because I have thought about it a great deal since.

It was two rooms. The front room had the counter, a bench for waiting, a rack of forms — dog licences, culvert permits, the tithe schedule for the coming season, which was a single sheet with the dates of the four collections and the hours the hall would be open. Behind the counter there was a filing cabinet, grey, four drawers, with a small brass frame on each drawer holding a typed card. The cards said, from the top: CURRENT. PRIOR. ARCHIVE. ORDERS.
The back room was smaller and had a window that gave onto the yard, and in it there was a desk of plain wood, and a chair, and on the desk a ledger.

That was all. That was the whole apparatus of the thing. I had come three hundred miles on the strength of an advertisement, and what waited for me at the end of it was a room the size of a pantry with a desk in it, and a woman in a cardigan going on about tea.

I say all this because I have read accounts — you understand that I have had a great deal of time to read, latterly — of people who walked into some room or other and felt the wrongness of it immediately, felt the air change, knew. I did not know. I felt nothing except that it was smaller than I expected and that the radiator was on too high. If there is a lesson in this account, and I am not certain there is, it is that the thing does not announce itself. It has a counter. It has a rack of forms. It has an order book for stationery, and I have seen the order book, and the ledgers are item fourteen, and they cost less than you would think.
She showed me the desk that first evening, before the tea had properly gone cold, because she could see I wanted to be shown.
"Now," she said. "The mechanics. It's simpler than people expect and I'd rather you had it from me than picked it up wrong."
She opened the ledger. It was ruled, and had a margin, and was three-quarters empty.

"They come in and they sit there" — the chair on the far side, which I had not registered as being on the far side of anything — "and they talk. And you write it down. That's it. That's the whole of it."
"In longhand."

"In longhand, in your own hand, in the book." She said this without any change of tone at all, and that is important, and I will come back to it. "It doesn't work typed. It doesn't work if someone else writes it for you. It doesn't work if you record it and write it up after. The hand has to be yours and it has to be at the time." She squared the ledger on the blotter. "The saying doesn't do anything on its own. People find that hard to credit — they come in wanting to unburden, and they think the unburdening's in the telling, and it isn't. What's spoken is just weather. It's the writing that moves it."
"Moves it where?"
And here is the thing about Adele Storr, which took me most of a year to see properly and which I have never been able to hate her for.
She said, "To you, dear," and she said it the way you would tell a new clerk which drawer the invoices go in.
There is a word for what I felt then and the word is relief.
I had come to Halloran with something of my own. I am going to set it down here in the plain way, because I have spent my whole life declining to, and because there is no longer any reason not to.

My mother was ill for nine years. I nursed her. There was no one else — my father had been dead a long while and my brother had a family in another country and sent money instead, which I understood, and which I have never in my life said a word against, and which sat in me like a stone for nine years.

What I did not expect, and what nobody warns you about, is that she came to hate me for it. Not for anything I did. For being there. For being the one who saw her not able to do things. Every kindness I did her was a fresh humiliation and there was no way to stop doing kindnesses, and so I humiliated her every day for nine years, four or five times a day, and she resented me for it with a purity that I think must have been the last strong thing she had.
She died in the March. I was thirty-four. I had a small amount of money and no one to tell.

So when Adele Storr said to you, dear, in that voice, over the tea, what went through me was not fear. It was a kind of lifting. I thought — and I remember the shape of the thought exactly — at last, a use. I thought: I have been absorbing things for nine years and nobody was collecting them and here is a place with a desk and a book and a schedule and a wage, and a whole town that will hand me its griefs and thank me.
I thought that carrying would be the opposite of being alone.

I want that on the record before anything else, because everything that follows is easier to bear if you understand that nobody tricked me. The advertisement was accurate. Adele Storr was truthful. The mechanism was explained to me on the first evening, over tea, in a room with a radiator on too high, and I said yes with my whole chest.
"There's one more piece," she said, "and then I'll let you sleep."

She went out to the front room and came back with a cup. Not a cup in any ceremonial sense — a plain white thing, the kind you get six of. There was perhaps two inches of liquid in it, dark, still faintly warm, and the smell of it came up at me like something out of a hedgerow: bitter, green, with a metal edge underneath.
"What is it?"

"It's what we give you." She set it down. "It's for the hands, mostly. You'll find you cramp. Every Taker cramps, it's the writing, hours of it. This settles that." She pushed it half an inch towards me. "Before each session. Not after, it's no good after. Before."
"What's in it?"

"I couldn't tell you the half of it," said Adele Storr, cheerfully, and I have thought about that sentence for three years. Because it was true. She could not have told me. She had administered that cup twice a season for thirty years and she did not know what was in it and had never asked, and the reason she had never asked is that it was on the order form, item nine, between the ink and the blotting paper.
I drank it.
It was foul, and then it was not, and then about eleven minutes later — I counted, out of habit — the walls of the room went a very small distance further away from me than they had been.

That is the closest I can get to it. People want a description of colours and there are no colours. What the cup does is it takes away a thing you did not know you had, which is the skin between you and the room. Not the skin on your body. The other one. The one that means that when a person across a table is unhappy, you observe that they are unhappy, and it stays theirs.

That went. And what came in its place was Adele Storr sitting three feet away from me, and I could feel — with no image and no words and nothing you could call thought — that she was tired, and pleased with me, and worried about a thing to do with her son that had nothing to do with any of this, and that under all of it she was a fundamentally contented woman who had been contented her whole life and did not know that this was rare.
I said, "Oh."
"Yes," said Adele. "It's a lot the first time. It settles."
She gave me the back pages that night, and I have come to think of this as the cruellest hour of my life, though nothing happened in it at all.

"Every Taker writes a last entry," she said. "When they're done. It's the tradition and it's also practical — you'll want to know who came before you. They're all in the archive drawer. Take them up with you."
There were nine.
I sat on the bed in the room above the wool shop, which the Office rented for me, and I read nine final entries by nine people who had held my post since 1911, and I understood not one thing.
Not because they were cryptic. Because I could not read them.

The first three were legible. A man called Aldous Brant, 1911 to 1919, who wrote in a copperplate that got shakier over four lines and complained, at the end, about a dog. A woman called Sylvie Oduya, 1919 to 1931, who wrote two sentences about her sister. A man whose name I could not make out at all, 1931 to 1938, four words.

And then it went. The later hands went. By the 1960s the entries were three or four words got down with enormous effort in letters an inch high, and by the last of them — Marguerite Sayers, retired 1979 — it was a single word which I took for cold and which was not, and I know now what it was, and I am not going to write it.
I sat with those nine pages and what I thought was: how sad. I thought: these were old people at the end of long service and their hands had failed them, the way hands do.
I did not think: these are the only nine people who ever knew what I am about to know, and each of them had one page, and each of them chose what to spend it on, and not one of them chose to warn me.

I have thought about that a great deal since. I have concluded that it was not cowardice, or not only cowardice. I think that by the time you have a page, you no longer have the hand. And I think that is not an accident either, though I cannot prove it, and there is no one left to ask.
My first collection was on a Tuesday, at nine in the morning, and it was a woman named Doreen Callas, and it was about a fence.

She was seventy-one. She had a coat on though the hall was warm. She sat down in the chair on the far side of the desk and put her handbag on her knees and held it with both hands like something that might get away, and she said, "Do I just start?"
"Whenever you like."
She talked for forty minutes.

The fence was between her property and the property of a man named Vergil Doak, and it had been put in wrong in 1974, and it was wrong by somewhere between eleven and fourteen inches depending on where you measured, and she had measured it in eleven places, and she recited all eleven, and the recitation took nine minutes.
I wrote it down.

Then she told me about the letter she had written in 1976, and the letter she had received, and the phrasing of the letter she had received, which she could still quote, and she quoted it. Then she told me about Doak's wife, who was dead now, and who had once said something at a church function about Doreen's mother that Doreen had never repeated to anybody, and which she now repeated to me, and which was so small that I had to write it twice to be sure I had it right.

Somewhere around the thirty-minute mark I understood that the fence was not the subject. The subject was that Doreen Callas had been a person to whom a wrong was done in 1974 and no one had ever agreed with her about it, and she had carried the un-agreed-with-ness of it for forty-nine years, and it had become the shape of her.
I wrote that down too. I wrote it all down. My hand ached from the second page onward and I kept going because she was still talking, and because it did not occur to me that I was permitted to stop.

And at the fortieth minute she stopped, and sat back, and said, "Well," and looked around the room as if she had just come into it. Her face had changed. Not dramatically. She looked like a woman who had put down two bags of shopping.
"Is that all right?" she said. "Was that all right? I do go on."
"That's what it's for."

"You're a nice girl," said Doreen Callas, and she meant it, and she took her handbag and she went out into the morning and I have seen her many times since and she has never once mentioned the fence to me or to anyone, because it is not in her any more. It is in the book, and it is in me, and Doreen Callas is a cheerful woman of seventy-four who is very good with her grandchildren.
I sat in the little room for a while afterward.

I did not feel ill. I want to be precise, because precision is all I have to offer. I did not feel ill and I did not feel burdened and there was no moment of arrival. What there was, was this: I sat in the chair after she had gone, and I found that I was thinking about the fence.
Not remembering it. Thinking about it. Turning it over. Getting angry, in a small idling way, about eleven to fourteen inches of ground I had never seen belonging to a woman I had met once.
And I thought — and this is the last unclouded thought I can find in the whole of that year — well, that's natural. You've just sat through forty minutes of it. It'll pass.

It did not pass. Nothing passes. That is the entire discovery of my life and it took me two years and a woman's death to arrive at it, and I could have had it on the first Tuesday, in a warm room, for nothing.
I saw Ottmar Lisk for the first time that same week, across the square, and I did not know what I was looking at.

There was a man of about seventy standing outside the wool shop, quite still, looking at the window display. He was well dressed. He had a good coat. He was standing with his hands held slightly away from his body, the way you hold your hands when they have been in cold water.
Adele was with me. She said, "That's Ottmar. You'll want to know him."
"He's the other one?"
"He's the one before you." She said it without lowering her voice. "Nine years. He's very near the end of it now, poor lamb, he'll be relieved in the autumn. He's earned it."
Relieved.

I looked at him across the square for perhaps four seconds. He did not look at us. His hands, held out at that slight angle, were the wrong colour and the wrong shape, and I registered that, and I filed it as arthritis, because arthritis is a thing that happens to men of seventy, and because the alternative had not yet been offered to me and I am not clever enough to have invented it on my own.
He would be relieved in the autumn. He had earned it. There would be a small good house at the edge of town.
Everything I was told was true.

The road. It goes round. There was never any need for it to go round, there's nothing there, it's flat as a plate, and it adds a mile and a half each way and it has done since before I was born and nobody will say why. I've asked. They say it's always gone round.
Also my son-in-law.

It is the not mentioning that I cannot get past — the way we have both agreed, without agreeing, that it is not a thing, and I am the only one of us doing the agreeing, and she gets to be a person who does not owe anybody anything, and I get to be a person who is fine about it, and I have been fine about it for two years.

PART TWO
THE TITHERS
There is a rhythm to a collection season and it took me one full turn of the year to learn it.

The hall opens at nine. The schedule is posted in the Office window and in the church porch and at the garage, and people come more or less when they are told to come, in the order of the register, which is alphabetical and has been since 1911. Four days for A through F. Four for G through L. And so on. Two weeks in the spring, two in the summer, two in the autumn, two in the winter, and in the between-times you have the filing to do, and the previous season to index, and nothing else at all.

Four thousand one hundred and six people. Not all of them come — children under fourteen do not, and there are perhaps three hundred adults in any given season who do not bother, and there is one household that has never come, and I will get to that.
Call it three thousand two hundred sittings a year. Call it four a day, five in a heavy week. Call it forty minutes each and some of them two hours.
I got very good at it very quickly, and that was the problem, and nobody told me it was the problem because from where they stood it did not look like one.
Here is what I learned about the work in the first summer.

The first thing is that you cannot ration. I tried. Around the fourth week I started doing a thing where I let the words come in at a slight distance — nodding, writing, keeping my attention a little bit above the desk. It is what a doctor does. It is what a priest does. It is a professional skill and I had assumed it was the professional skill of this job as well.

It does not work. What I found was that on the days I did that, the writing came out fine and the ledger filled up and nothing transferred at all. The grievance stayed where it was. Doreen Callas's fence had come into me because for forty minutes I had genuinely and stupidly cared about eleven to fourteen inches of a stranger's ground.

That is the mechanism. It is not the ink and it is not the cup, quite. The cup takes the wall down; the hand does the moving; but the thing that has to be there in the middle is that you feel it as they felt it, at full weight, without discount. If you do not, you are a clerk. If you do, you are a Taker.

Which means that the qualification for this work is the one quality that guarantees it will destroy you. They do not hire the strong. There is no strength involved anywhere in it. They hire the porous.
The second thing I learned is that carrying admits no hierarchy.

I want to be exact about this because it is the part that people cannot believe. I sat, in one Thursday of that first summer, with a man who told me for fifty minutes about his neighbour's wind chimes; and then with a woman who told me, in a flat voice, in four minutes, what her uncle had done to her in a car in 1961 and what her mother had said about it afterwards.
I wrote them both down in the same hand in the same book.

And they arrived in me at the same density. That is the truth of it and it is the thing I still cannot get anyone to understand. There is no scale. There is no valve that opens wider for the uncle than for the wind chimes. The apparatus takes what is given at the weight the giver gives it, and the man with the wind chimes had a grievance that occupied the whole of his available capacity for grievance, and so it came in at the whole of mine.

I carry both of those. I have carried them for three years. If you asked me now, sitting here, which of them presses harder, I could not tell you, and there is no version of me left that thinks that is an acceptable answer.
I want to give one sitting whole, from the inside, so the reader knows what the work actually was. I will give the foreman, because he was ordinary, and ordinary is the point.

His name was Aldo Pruitt and he ran the crew at the grain store and he came in on a Wednesday in his work clothes, having plainly decided that changing would have made it an occasion. He sat with his cap on his knee. He was perhaps sixty. He said, "I don't have much."
They all say that. It is a courtesy, like wiping your feet.

Then he said that he had run that floor for twenty-two years. That in twenty-two years the store had never once lost a contract over weight or spoilage, which was him, that was his doing, the checking was his and the system for the checking was his. That three managers had come and gone above him in that time and each of them had been thanked at a dinner. That there had never been a dinner for him, and he had never wanted one, he wanted that understood, he was not a man who wanted dinners.

"But you notice," he said. "That's the thing of it. You'd think it would wear out, the noticing. It's twenty-two years. And every time the wagon goes out clean I notice that nobody knows it went out clean because of me, and the noticing is as fresh as the first day. It doesn't wear. Why doesn't it wear?"

And here is what the work is. The cup was in me and the wall was down, and so I did not hear that question the way you have just read it. It came across the desk with its whole weight — twenty-two years of a man standing on a cold floor at five in the morning being excellent at something in front of nobody — and because the wall was down it was not his twenty-two years by the time it reached me. It was simply twenty-two years, unowned, looking for a place to stand. And my pen was moving. And the place it found was me.

You feel it go in. I have tried many ways of saying this and the truest is the plainest: it is like swallowing when your throat is sore. There is a moment of resistance, and a moment of passage, and then a weight has changed rooms, and the man across the desk feels the weight change rooms — you watch it cross his face like weather clearing — and he straightens, and looks about himself, and says something like well, and picks his cap up off his knee.
Aldo Pruitt stood at the door and said, "I don't know what you did, but thank you," and went back to the grain store.

And I sat and noticed, freshly, as if it were mine, because it now was, that nobody knew the wagons went out clean because of me. I carried a resentment about a grain store I had never entered. I carry it tonight. It has not worn. He was right about that. It does not wear.
Adele took me to lunch at the end of the summer season and told me I was doing wonderfully.

We sat in the window of the place on the square. She had the soup. She said, "I'll tell you what everyone's saying, and then I'll stop, because it'll go to your head. They're saying it's the best it's felt in years."
"The town?"

"The town." She broke a roll. "You get a — there's a texture to a season, you'll learn to feel it. Some years the collection goes through and everyone's a bit flat afterwards, and you can tell it didn't take properly. And some years it's like this. Everyone's light. My sister-in-law spoke to me at the fete for the first time since 1998." She laughed, delighted, entirely herself. "You're filling wonderfully, Ruth. Ottmar was never this quick."
I said thank you.

I have gone back to that sentence perhaps a thousand times. You're filling wonderfully. She was paying me a compliment. She was not being sly, she was not enjoying a secret, she was a woman of sixty in a soup restaurant telling a young colleague that she was good at her job, and the thing she was praising me for was the rate at which I was being consumed.

And the horror of Adele Storr — I have arrived at this slowly and I hold it now without any anger, which is itself a symptom — is that she was not concealing the second half of the sentence. There was no second half in her. She had administered this office for thirty years and she had never asked what was in the cup and she had never asked where the load went at the end and she had never asked why the qualification was kinlessness. Not because she suspected and looked away. Because it had never presented itself to her as a thing that had a question in it.

She was, I think, the most contented woman I have ever met, and she had been made that way on purpose, and so had everybody else, and that is the whole crime and it does not have a criminal in it that you could point at.
I met my own life in a stranger's mouth in the September.
Her name was Wynn Tavish and she was fifty-eight and she had come in about a boundary hedge, which is what she said at the door, and then she sat down and did not talk about the hedge.
She talked about her mother.

Six years, she said. She had done six years of it. There was a brother in Perth. The brother sent money and rang at Christmas, and she had never in her life said a word against him and did not intend to start now. And her mother had hated her for it. Not for anything she did — for being the one who was there. For being the witness. Every cup of tea was an insult and there was no way to stop bringing the tea.

"She was a good woman," Wynn Tavish said. "I want that written down as well. She was a good woman and she hated me and both of those are true and I've never been able to put them in the same sentence out loud."
I wrote it down.
I wrote it in my own hand, at the time, in the book, with the cup in me and the wall down, feeling it exactly as she felt it, which is the only way it works.

Here is what I had believed, without ever quite articulating it, since the first evening over the tea: that this office was a kind of exchange. That I gave and received in the same coin. That because I was a person who had carried something, carrying other people's would be a sort of company for it — that there would be a levelling, a fellowship, a me too that did some quiet work on the original.

There is no exchange. I sat there with my hand going and I found that I now had two of it. The hand went in the second winter, and it went the way Adele had said it would, which is to say gradually and then as a fact.

First it was cramp after a long sitting, which I had been promised and which the cup was supposed to settle and did. Then it was cramp that did not go by the evening. Then, one morning in the January, I woke and my right hand was shut and I could not open it with my left, and I lay in the dark and worked at it for something like a quarter of an hour before it came, and when it came it hurt in a way that had nothing to do with muscle.
After that it never entirely opened again. There is a degree of hook that is now simply the shape of my hand and it arrived that January and it did not leave.
Sleep went at about the same time, and sleep went differently, and I did not have a word for what replaced it until much later.

What happens is that you lie down and you are not alone. There is no voice and there is no vision. There is a room, and in the room there is you, and there is also the residue of three thousand two hundred sittings, and it does not speak, it just occupies. It is the sensation of a full house with the lights off. You are aware, without any content, that a great many people are extremely unhappy about a great many small things, and that all of them are inside the same body as you, and that they are not going anywhere.

I stopped sleeping in the dark. I want to be honest about the small indignities as well as the large ones. I slept with the lamp on for the last two years of my service, like a child, and Adele found out and had a second lamp sent over from the Office, and did not make anything of it, and I want that written down too.
Two sittings from that winter, because they belong here.

The first was a girl of nineteen called Nella Ferrand — the daughter of the poplar woman, though I did not connect them at the time — who came in with her coat zipped to the chin and sat on the front edge of the chair and said nothing for six minutes. I have learned to let the six minutes happen. The ones who take longest to start are carrying the realest things, and they are checking the room, and what they are checking it for is whether the promise is true: that you can say the thing here, the actual thing, and it will be taken from you and no one will ever hand it back.
What she finally said was that she did not love her own child.

She said it in one sentence, with the flat delivery, and then she watched my pen to make sure I was writing it, and then it came in a flood — that the birth had gone wrong, that her body had been a long time mending and had not mended all the way and never would, that she loved the child completely, she wanted that written too, write that it's also true, and that every day some part of her did the arithmetic of what the child had cost and resented the answer, and that she had carried both of those in the same chest for two years and there was no person alive she could have said it to, because there is no way to say it that does not sound like a monster saying it.
"But you have to say it to somebody," said Nella Ferrand, nineteen years old, "or it goes bad. My gran told me that. She said that's what the hall is for."

I wrote it, and it went into me the way they all go into me, and she cried for a minute, and then she stopped, and the loose thing happened to her face, and she zipped her coat down two inches, which I have thought about ever since, and thanked me, and went out to the pram she had left with a neighbour by the door.

She will be a good mother. I mean that without any shadow on it. She goes home from that hall able to love the child with the whole of the room the resentment was standing in. That is what the Tithe buys, and I was the coin, and I want the ledger of this account to show both columns.

The second sitting was an old man named Harmon Voss, and it was about the war, and I will give it two sentences. I understood him completely, and I wrote it down, and it has sat in me since beside everything else, at the same weight as the wind chimes, which is the obscenity of my condition and the last time I will mention it.

"They don't come," Adele had said.

And what it seeped into was the filing.

Because I had by then written down, in my own hand, something on the order of six thousand grievances. And there was a category I had never named, because it did not look like a category. It looked like the ordinary friction of a rural county.
The road that goes round.
The survey markers on the north side.
The signage, which the county had changed in 1998, and which eleven separate people had complained about with a heat entirely out of proportion to signage.

The Storr name on the school, which four people had raised in two years, each of them apologetically, each of them saying some version of I know it's petty, I know they gave the money, I just don't like seeing it.
A drainage ditch on the west boundary that three farmers wanted moved and could not say why it bothered them.

The poplars in the east field, planted in that too-straight line, which a woman named Ferrand had spent twenty minutes on, and at the end of the twenty minutes had said: "It's a fence. That's what it is. It's somebody's fence and it's not a fence, and I can't look at it."
I sat with my index cards in the back room in the March and I laid them out and they were all the same complaint.

Every single one of them was about a boundary. About a line drawn on the ground. About where a thing stops being one person's and starts being another's — and every one of them was angry, and none of them could say what about.
So I went into the archive drawer.

The Tithe Office keeps everything. That is the thing about an operation that thinks of itself as clerical: it has no instinct for destroying evidence, because it does not believe there is any. Ninety years of ledgers, bound, indexed, in a grey cabinet in a room off the square, and the key hangs on a nail behind the door, and it has hung there for as long as anyone can remember, because who would want them.

I read backwards. I did it at night, and it took me from the March to the June, and I was reading with a hand that no longer worked and eyes that were going, and I did it in the wrong order — I started at 1979 and went back to 1911 — and I am glad I did, because forwards I might have missed it.

I want to describe those nights, because they were the strangest work of my life and because the reader should know what it is to read a town's whole inner history in the dark with a magnifying glass.

You take a ledger down and it has a smell — paper and dust and something underneath the dust that I came to think of as the smell of the ink itself, though it cannot have been. You open it anywhere and a voice starts. That is what shocked me first: they are voices. Every Taker before me had done what I did, which is get it down word for word in the rhythm it was said, because the rhythm is part of the weight, and so a woman dead sixty years complains to you about a copper boiler in her own cadence, with her own repetitions, and you can hear her, you can hear which words she leaned on. I sat in the back room at midnight with the lamp and a rug over my knees and I listened to Halloran talk in its sleep for three months.

And the town does not change. That was the second shock. The clothes change and the prices change and the boiler becomes a washing machine, and underneath, season upon season, decade upon decade, it is the same town saying the same things. The brother is always given the farm. The loan is always unmentioned. Someone is always passed over, someone is always not touched, someone always cannot sit at the table. I had thought, in my first year, that I was collecting the particular sorrows of particular people. I was not. I was taking the same tithe the last nine of us took, from the same crop, off the same ground.

Some nights I read a whole year in a sitting. Some nights I managed four pages, because the hand that had written them was a late hand — a full hand — and reading a full hand is slow, and something else besides slow that I did not have a word for then. You are watching a person drown in increments of a season. In the spring their letters have a small tremble. By the autumn the tremble has a stagger in it. You turn fifty pages and a year of their life has gone into the book and the writing at the back is a ruin of the writing at the front, and then a new year starts in a new ledger and it is worse, and you know — you alone, of everyone who ever lived, because nobody else has ever read these — you know exactly where this hand is going, and you turn the pages toward it anyway.
Here is what I found.
The same complaints. In every hand. In every decade.
The road goes round. 1974. 1961. 1952. 1948. 1933. 1919. The same road, the same goes round, the same inability to say why it should not.
The markers. Every generation. Somebody always thinks the markers have been moved, and photographs them, and is thought a crank.

The signage complaint is new because the signage is new, but its grandfather is a complaint from 1931 about the county renaming the west road, and its great-grandfather is a complaint from 1914 about a milestone.
And under all of them, running the whole ninety years like a watermark, the boundary. Where the line is. Who put the line there. Whether the line is right.
Never once the thing itself.

Not one entry, in ninety years, in six ledgers, in maybe two hundred thousand grievances, that said: this land was taken. Not one that said a name. Not one that said my grandmother, or the treaty, or the people who were here. Not one that said before.

You understand that this is not what an archive of a town's private anger looks like. An archive of a town's private anger contains everything. I had the uncle in the car. I had a man who resented his wife for chewing and a woman who resented her own knee. There was no subject too small and no subject too shameful; the whole apparatus is built on the promise that you can say the thing you cannot say.
And in ninety years of people saying the thing they cannot say, nobody had said the only thing that was actually unsayable.

That is not silence. Silence has a shape you can see. This was an absence with pressure behind it — a hole with the edges pushed up all around, the way a hole is when something has been pulled out of the ground rather than never planted.
They were all angry about it. All four thousand of them, in every generation, continuously, for ninety years. The anger was completely intact. The anger came in every season by the bucket.
It just had nowhere to be pointed. So it went at the road, and the markers, and the sign, and the poplars, and the name over the school door.

I asked what the land was called before.
