PART FOUR
THE CUP
I skipped the cup on a Tuesday in the spring of my third year, and I did it out of nothing more elevated than temper.

The tin was empty. It comes over from the Office in a tin, made up somewhere I never asked about, and it sits on the shelf in the back room, and that morning there was a scale of dried sediment in the bottom and nothing else. And I stood there with my hooked hand and my two years and I thought: well, then I won't, in exactly the spirit of a woman who has decided not to take her coat.
The first sitting was a man called Ivo Rennick, and it was about his sister-in-law, and it took thirty-five minutes.
I wrote it all down. I got every word. It was, if anything, a better record than usual, because I could hear the sentences as sentences instead of as weather coming in.
And when he stood up he had not put anything down.

I saw it happen — or rather, I saw it not happen. There is a moment at the end of a sitting where a person's face comes loose. Doreen Callas had it on my first morning. It is quite unmistakable once you have seen three thousand of them. Ivo Rennick got to the end of his thirty-five minutes and sat back and waited for it, and it did not come, and he looked around the room with a small confusion, and said, "Right," and then said, "Right," again, and went out into the street still carrying every ounce of it.
And I sat in the chair with my hand aching and nothing new in me at all, and I thought: oh.

I understood the mechanism in about four seconds, sitting there, and it was the first thing in two years I had understood on time rather than late. It was never the writing on its own. It was never the sitting or the hall or the ledger. The cup takes down the skin between you and the room, and without the skin down you are simply a woman with a pen taking a statement, and the grievance goes home in the man who brought it.
I did nine more sittings that day, dry, and I am going to give the reader that afternoon, because it was the only ordinary working day of my life and I have polished it like a stone.

A woman came in about her sister's will and I listened to her. I do not mean I heard her; I had heard everybody for two years, at full weight, from the inside. I mean I sat across a desk from another person and her trouble stayed on her side of it, and from my side I could see it whole — see the shape of it, see the places where she was wrong about it and the one place where she was terribly right — the way you can see a field from a stile that you cannot see from inside the wheat. I had opinions. I had never once had an opinion during a sitting; there is no room for opinions when the thing is coming into you. I thought: she should write to the solicitor and stop writing to the sister. I nearly said it. I am told that is what a counsellor is.

A man came in about his neighbour's dog and he was funny about it — he had jokes, it was a performance he had clearly given at the garage — and I laughed. Out loud, at a sitting. He was delighted. Nobody had ever laughed in that hall; they come out of it lighter but nobody has ever once come out of it laughed-with, because the apparatus does not attend to the telling, only to the weight, and a joke weighs what its grievance weighs.

All afternoon the town came and sat and talked, and all afternoon their sorrows stood in the room like furniture instead of climbing into my chest, and I heard more, understood more, could have helped more, than in two years of taking. And every one of them went home carrying exactly what they had brought.

I walked back along the field road in the evening light with an ordinary quantity of unhappiness in me — mine, which is to say nine years of my mother — and it felt like almost nothing. It felt like a coat. I remember stopping by the poplars and standing there in the level sun for a while for no reason at all, which is a thing I had not done since I arrived, because you do not stand about admiring the light when there are four thousand people in you.
It was the happiest four hours since I was thirty-four. I want it recorded. And I want recorded what it cost, which is the next thing.
The thinning started on the Friday.

I did not connect it at first. What I noticed was that the woman in the wool shop was short with a customer over an order, and that there were raised voices at the garage, and that a man crossing the square in front of me stopped and turned round and said something to another man about a car, and the other man said something back, and neither of them was drunk and it was eleven in the morning.

By the Sunday, two families on the west road were not speaking. By the Monday there was an actual argument outside the church, out loud, in front of people, about a chair that had been taken out of a hall in 1997.
It took me until the Monday evening to understand what I was looking at, and when I did understand it I had to sit down on the step of the Office with my head down.
Nine people. I had let nine people go home with what they came in with, out of temper, over an empty tin, and by the following weekend the town's temperature had come up like a fever.

That is the arithmetic of Halloran and I had never once seen it laid out. Four thousand people. Three thousand two hundred sittings a year. That pleasantness — the thing visitors remark on, the thing that made Adele's sister-in-law speak to her at the fete for the first time since 1998 — is not a culture and it is not a character and it is certainly not a virtue.
It is a maintenance schedule. And I was the plant. And nine skipped units of throughput had put a visible crack in it inside of seventy-two hours.
Adele came round on the Tuesday with a fresh tin.
I want to set down exactly how she did it, because it is the last thing I will ever say in her defence and it is also the entire indictment.

She came into the back room and put the tin on the shelf and said, "That was my fault entirely, the order went in late, I've had a word with myself." And then she said, "You did nine without it, didn't you."
"I did."
"I thought so." She was folding the paper the tin had come in. She was not angry. There was no edge on it anywhere. "You'll cramp something dreadful tomorrow. It really is much better before."
And I looked at her — at this kind, competent, contented woman folding brown paper in a small room — and I said, "Adele, what does it do?"
"It settles the hands."
"It doesn't settle the hands. My hands are ruined. It's never once settled my hands."
And Adele Storr said, "Well, it's what it's for," and put the folded paper in her bag, and asked whether I wanted anything picked up in town.

That is not evasion. I need the reader to sit with this, because it is the hardest thing in this account to credit and it is the true one. There was nothing behind that sentence. She was not steering me off. She was answering the question with the whole of what was in her, and the whole of what was in her was: it's for the hands; it's item nine on the order form; it goes between the ink and the blotting paper.
Thirty years. Twice a season. She had handed that cup to two people across three decades and watched what became of both of them, and she had never had the thought.

And why would she. She came to the collections herself. She sat in the chair every season like everybody else and gave me hers — and hers were good ones, they were real, she was not a shallow woman — and she went out lighter. Whatever capacity she might once have had for looking at that cup and saying hold on, she had been bringing it to me twice a year and I had been writing it down.
You cannot investigate a thing you are structurally unable to resent. That is the whole of Halloran. That is the machine's only defence and it has never needed another one.
Ottmar Lisk died in the January of my third year, fourteen months after his relief, which the row will tell you is about the usual.
His last page came into the archive drawer in the February, and I did not go and look at it for nearly a month, and when I finally did I was not looking for what I found.

Here is what a final entry is, procedurally. When a Taker is relieved, they are given the back of the current ledger and they write their own grievance in it, in their own hand, like anybody else. It is described as a courtesy — the one entry you are permitted to make on your own behalf after a career of making them for other people. Adele called it the kindness at the end. Every one of my nine predecessors had taken it.

Lisk's was four words. I am not going to write them down; they were about a woman, and they were his, and he had nine years of everybody else's in him and he spent his one page on that, and I think it was the correct decision and I hope it did something for him.
What I looked at was the letters.

I had his early hand. I had ledgers going back to 1970 and Ottmar Lisk had been in that chair from 1970 to 1979 as a young man of thirty-two and his writing then was small, square, slightly backward-sloping, the hand of a person who had done some clerical work and was rather proud of it.
The four words on the last page were an inch high and had taken him, by the look of the ink, several minutes.

And I put my own hand next to it. The winter I had just finished. And there was no difference worth arguing about. His at nine years and mine at two and a half were the same handwriting, and the reason for that is that he had been a large calm man of seventy who was used to being disliked, and I was a woman of thirty-six who had spent nine years learning to absorb everything that was given to her without ever once putting any of it down.
They had hired me for that. It was on the criteria. A demonstrated history of absorbing without retaliating.
They call it temperament. It is a wound, and they advertise for it, and it is the single quality that makes a great Taker, and it is the reason a great Taker lasts a third as long as a mediocre one.
I was very good at my job. It is the only thing in my life I have ever been very good at and it killed me in three years.
I did the tally on a night in the April and it took me two hours and I have never recovered from it.
I need to explain the indexing first, plainly, because everything turns on it and it is the most boring thing in this book. That is not an apology. Its boringness is the whole disguise.

Every Taker indexes. It is half the work of the between-times — you go back through the completed season and you pull out the names. Not the names of the tithers; those are on the register already. The names mentioned. Every person complained about, in every sitting, goes onto a card with the page number beside it. The brother who got the farm has a card. Vergil Doak of the fence has a card. If eleven different people complain about the county signage there is no card, because signage is not a person; but if eleven different people complain about the same man, his card gets eleven page numbers, one at a time, season by season, in the Taker's own hand.

The cards go into the drawer marked PRIOR. At the end of each year they are consolidated onto a single sheet — every mentioned name, and beside each name the count of its mentions, ordered with the largest count at the top, because that is simply how a person orders a list and there is no other sensible way. The sheet goes into ARCHIVE. The cards are burned in the yard in a bucket, which I had done four times, warming my ruined hand at it, thinking nothing.

It is genuinely useful. I want that understood too. The Office fields queries — boundary disputes, probate, the county wanting to know who complained about the culvert — and the index answers them. No part of it was designed to look innocent. It is innocent, every single step of it, taken alone. You could explain each step to a magistrate and be thanked for your thoroughness.
That night I got out the sheets.

Ninety years of them. One per year. A column of names, and beside each name a number, and the whole thing ordered by the number, largest at the top, because that is how you would do it and there is no other sensible way.
1979. Top of the sheet, by a distance: a woman named Ilke Fanshawe. Under it, forty-one.
Marguerite Sayers was relieved in the September of 1979.
Ilke Fanshawe died in the September of 1979. I went into the county papers in the library the next morning and there she is, four inches, a fall at home, eighty-one, in declining health, no inquest.
1970. Top of the sheet: a man called Selwyn Doak. Thirty-six mentions. Relieved that year; died that year; a fall at home.
Nine reliefs in ninety years. Nine names at the top of a sheet. Nine falls at home.
And here is the thing that I have not been able to put down since and that I will carry out of this world with me: the sheet for the year of Ottmar Lisk's relief was in my handwriting.

I made it. In the October of my first year, in the back room, with my hand still mostly working, I went through the summer season and I pulled the names and I put them on cards and I consolidated them onto a single sheet in a neat descending column, and at the top of that column, at thirty-nine mentions, I wrote CORTLAND FREEM, and I did not know the man, and he was dead within the month.
I had loaded the gun. I had done it as filing. It had taken me about nine hours over three evenings and I had listened to the radio while I did it.
I spent two weeks after that night looking for the men in the room.

I want to give the reader those two weeks, because you will spend them too, if you have followed me this far, and I can save you the trouble. You will want a meeting. You will want a locked drawer, a second set of books, a Storr who knows. I wanted all of it, wanted it the way you want water — because if there is a meeting, then there are men in a room, and men in a room can be dragged out of it; a crime with an author has a door you can kick.

So I looked. I went through the ORDERS drawer invoice by invoice, and found stationery. I went through ninety years of the Office's correspondence with the county, and found culverts. I read the minutes of the parish council back to 1946, in the library, under Miss Pardoe's benevolent eye, and found a town arguing about gravel. I took Adele to lunch and asked her, straight out, over the soup, who decides when a Taker is relieved, and she said, "Decides? Love, it's when you're full. You'll know and I'll know. It's not a thing anyone decides, any more than the harvest is" — and there it was again, that answer with nothing behind it, that door opening onto a wall.

The founding families of Halloran did not build a court and they did not build a militia. I know what they built because I have read the instrument, and I will come to the instrument. They built a filing system, and then they had the one genuine piece of genius in this whole ninety-year machine, which is this: they made sure that nobody who operated it would ever understand it, by making its operation pleasant, and its records boring, and its single terrible output indistinguishable from an old person dying at home.
There is no conspiracy. There is nothing there to find.

Nobody chooses. There is no meeting. There is no man in a room with a list who says this one. The founding families of Halloran did not build a court and they did not build a militia; they built a filing system, and the filing system has an output, and the output is a name.
And what happens to that name is not an order either. That is the part that took me longest.

A Taker at relief has no self in her. I know that now from the inside and I will describe it when I come to it. What walks out of that hall at dusk is ninety seasons of other people's anger with the person burned out of the middle of it, and anger is not a mind, it does not deliberate, it does not select. It goes downhill. It goes to the lowest point in the landscape, and the lowest point in the landscape is whoever the town has been quietly, pettily, continuously complaining about for forty years.
The sheet does not aim anything. The sheet is a weather map. It tells you which way the water will run before the water runs.

Adele files it. That is her entire participation. She files it, and then, in the autumn, a thing happens at the north end of town and the paper says a fall at home, and Adele Storr is genuinely sorry about it and takes a casserole to the family.

Four thousand people elected Cortland Freem to die by finding him cold and standoffish and difficult over a period of decades, and not one of them voted, and not one of them knew there was an election, and every single one of them would have been horrified.
I want to say one more thing here and then I will stop.
I went and got the current year's cards. The ones I had been building since the January, unconsolidated, still loose in the PRIOR drawer.
I sat on the floor and I sorted them by hand, which took me until about four in the morning because my hand is what it is.
The name at the top was EMORY, and it was at forty-four, and the one under it was at nine.
She had asked me what the land was called before it was called Halloran, and I had said no, and she had told me that they always come back to her, and that not one of them had ever come back in time.

I was full. I had perhaps two months. I knew, that night, sitting on the floor of the Office at four in the morning with a card in my hand — I knew what I was for and I knew where I would be pointed and I knew who had built the landscape that would point me.
It made no difference at all. That is what I had not understood and could not have understood, and it is the last thing this account has to teach anybody.
Knowing is not a lever. There is no part of the apparatus that knowing touches.
PART FIVE
THE CROSSING
I began to leak in the May.

The first time was in the wool shop. I was buying nothing; I had got into the habit of standing in shops because a shop is a place where you can be near people without being sat across a desk from them. And a woman I did not know came in behind me and the bell went, and I turned round and said, in a voice that was not mine, "You've had that car across my drive since Thursday and I've not said a word."
The woman said, "Sorry?"
And I said, "Sorry," in my own voice, and went out.

It came about twice a week after that, then daily. Always somebody else's sentence, in somebody else's cadence, delivered at full sincerity by my own throat. I heard myself complain about a hedge. I heard myself, in the queue at the bank, begin an account of a christening in 1996 that I had taken down eleven months before from a woman who has since died.

That is what full means. There is no gauge on the side of a Taker. That is the gauge: when the thing starts coming out of you sideways, in other people's voices, in the street, you are done, and the Office knows what it means, and arrangements are made.
Adele made them the way you make a dental appointment.
"The eleventh," she said. "That's a Tuesday. Would a Tuesday suit?"
I said a Tuesday would suit.

"You'll want to put your things somewhere. Not that you'll want much of it after, people don't, but it's nice to have it done." She was writing in the desk diary. She had reading glasses on a chain by then. "And it's a dusk thing, so you'll have the whole day, and I'd say don't sit about with it. Ottmar did the crossword all day and I don't think it helped him."
I said, "Adele. What happens at a relief?"

And she looked up over the glasses with a face of such uncomplicated sympathy that I nearly put my head on the desk, and she said, "You're emptied, love. That's all it is. It all comes off you and you're done and you've earned it, and then there's the cottage and we look after you, and I'll come Sundays."
She believed every word.
I found the instrument of the Tithe four days before the eleventh, in the bottom of the ARCHIVE drawer, under the consolidated sheets, in a folder nobody had opened in my time.

It is nine pages, dated 1911, signed by four men, one of them a Storr. It is largely municipal — the establishment of the office, the terms of engagement, the wage, the rota, the requirement that the officer be of no local kin.

But there is a page at the front that is not municipal at all, and it does not read like a page written by county men in 1911, and I have come to believe it was copied out of something much older that one of them had got hold of and only half understood.

It uses the word asha, and it glosses it: the true order of a thing; how a matter actually stands. And against it, it sets druj, which it glosses as the Lie — and then, in a phrase I have thought about every day since, it says that the Lie is not a false saying but a disordering, a making of the world unrecognisable to those who stand in it.
It calls the office of the Taker a cup, and the drink a cup, and does not distinguish between them, and I do not think the distinction was ever intended.

It calls the walk at dusk the crossing, and there is a line about a bridge where a thing is weighed, and the sense of it — I am not a scholar, I am a woman with a hooked hand reading a document at two in the morning — the sense of it is that the crossing is where the account is settled and the weight is read off, and that what goes over the bridge is not the person but the load.

And on the last line of that page there is a word set apart, which the document does not gloss, and which is the name of the thing a full vessel becomes when it is opened at the end. I found it later in a library book. It is the name of the daeva of fury. The old texts say he carries a bloodied club and that he is not a spirit of anger as we would understand anger — not the anger of a man at a fence — but wrath with nobody inside it. Wrath that has been separated from any person who could be angry.

They had the whole thing. In 1911. Written down, glossed, filed, and put in a drawer with an order form for stationery, and ninety years of Storrs administered it as a public convenience and nobody ever read to the bottom of the first page.
That is the Lie in the document's own sense. Not a false thing said. A true thing made unrecognisable by the cabinet it was put in.
Mrs Emory came to the Office on the Monday, the day before.
She did not sit down. She stood in the doorway of the back room with her coat on and looked at me for a while, and what she said first was, "You came back."
"You said everyone does."
"In time, I said. Not one in time." She looked at my hand. She looked at it frankly, the way nobody in Halloran ever looked at it. "You're for tomorrow."
"Yes."
"And you know where you're going."
"Yes."
"Well," said Mrs Emory. "That's more than any of the others managed."
And then she said the thing that I have taken apart a thousand times since and cannot get to come out any other way.

She said: "Don't be frightened of it and don't be sorry about it. I've had eighty-four years and forty of them were spent getting this. You're not doing something to me. You're the only door left in this town and it's taken me my whole life to get you built."
I said — and I want this written down, because it is the one thing I did — I said, "Then come now. Come and sit in the chair and tell me now, while I can still write."

And Mrs Emory said, "It doesn't work now. You're full. There's not a thimble of room in you and there hasn't been since the winter." She pulled her coat straight. "It has to be after. After, you're empty. That's the only hour in ninety years when there's anywhere in this town to put a thing and have it stay put."
Then she went home and put her house in order, and I sat in the back room until it got dark.
They came for me at seven on the Tuesday and it was the whole of the Office, which is Adele and a man called Petrie who does the accounts.

The hall was open and the lamps were on and there were perhaps thirty people in it, which surprised me. I had thought it was kept small. It is kept small in the sense that there is no announcement; but people know, and they come, and they stood along the wall in their coats with their hands in front of them and they were not ghoulish and they were not ashamed. It was the face people have at a retirement. It was, precisely and exactly, gratitude.
Doreen Callas was there. She was seventy-six by then. She had brought me a plant.

Adele read the verse. It is read at the head of every collection and I had heard it eleven times and I had never once heard it, and standing in the middle of that floor at dusk with my coat off I heard it, every line, and there is not one word in it that is untrue and there is not one word in it that is not a confession.
The town was never made to hold.
Blessed the ground that answers to one name.
And we will walk you out at dusk, and still your hands.
Thirty people said it with her. They have said it four times a year their whole lives, the way you say the words at a wedding.
Then Petrie brought the cup.

It was a double measure. I had never seen more than the two inches. It came up over the join in the glaze and there was a skin on it and the smell of it filled the whole space between me and the far wall.
And here is the last thing I have to tell about myself as a person, and then there is only the other.
I took it in both hands, and my hands were shaking, and I was not afraid.

I wanted it. I had wanted it for eleven months. I had four thousand people in me and no room and no sleep and a hand that would not open, and somebody was standing in front of me offering to take the wall down all the way, all the way, not the two inches, and I drank it the way you drink water after a fever.

I have gone over and over whether that is forgivable. I have not got anywhere with it. It is simply true. I went to that woman's house that night gladly, and no part of me was made to, and the last thing I did as myself was reach out for the cup with both hands.
The crossing is eleven hundred yards. I had walked it a hundred times.

You go out the side of the hall and down past the equipment yard and onto the field road, and the poplars are on your left in their too-straight line, and the town's lights come on behind you one at a time as the dusk comes down, and ahead of you at the end of it there are four small good houses and only one of them has a light on.
I remember the first two hundred yards.

I remember that the wall did not come down the way it did with the two inches. With the two inches it goes out to the edges of the room. This went out past the edges of the field. I could feel the town behind me — not the buildings, the people, all of them, four thousand and six of them, at once, the whole ordinary awful chorus of it, the fences and the loans and the chewing and the uncle and the knee, and it did not come into me because there was no longer an into.
I want to be very careful here. There was no vision and no roaring and nothing that would make a scene in a picture. What there was, was subtraction.

The self is a small thing and it is doing constant work. That is what I learned. It is the thing that stands between what is in you and what you do about it, and it works every second of your life, and you never once notice it, and when it goes what you notice is not the going. What you notice is how easy everything has become.
Somewhere around the poplars I stopped being anybody, and there was no moment of it, and I did not mind.
I am going to write what happened at the cottage. I have been three years getting to it and I am not going to be coy at the end.

The door was not locked. She was in the front room in a chair facing the door with the lamp on and her hands in her lap, and she had put her hair up and she was wearing good clothes, and she had been sitting like that, I think, for a long time.
She looked up and she said, "There you are."

What came through that door was not angry with her. That is the thing I most need to set down. There was no hatred in it, because hatred requires somebody to do the hating, and there was nobody in me at all. What there was, was a gradient — the whole ninety-year weight of a town's stored resentment finding, at last, after all those decades of running at roads and markers and poplars, an object that the count had made lower than everything around it.
It went to her the way water goes to a drain.
She did not get up and she did not put her hands out. I have that clearly. She sat and she watched it come and her face did not change.
The first thing was the chair going over.

I was strong. That is the detail I have never been able to make anybody understand and it is the one that wakes me. I am a woman of thirty-seven with a ruined hand and I could not carry a full kettle in the March, and that night I lifted an eighty-four-year-old woman and the chair she was sitting in together off the floor and took them into the wall, and it was nothing, it was like putting down a bag.
The lamp went. There was still light from the hall.

I did it with my hands. I want that on the record too, because there was a poker in that room and I have thought about why not the poker, and I think it is because there was no intention anywhere in it and a poker requires an intention. Hands do not. Hands are what the body reaches for when there is nobody home.
Her glasses went across the floor and I remember hearing them go and I remember that the sound was interesting.

It took a long time. It was not one blow and a stillness; that is a thing from films. She was small and she was old and she went on being alive far longer than seems possible, and there was a period in the middle of it — I do not know how long, and there is no possible way for me to know — when she had stopped being able to make a sound and had not stopped moving, and I went on, and I went on, and there was nothing in the whole world that could have made me stop, because stopping is a thing a person does and there was no person there.
And it felt —
I have to write this. This is the entire book and if I flinch here I have written nothing.
It felt marvellous.

It felt like the best thing that has ever happened to me. It felt like putting down four thousand people. It felt like sleep after eleven months of no sleep, like the hand opening, like being emptied out with warm water, like being forgiven — that is the closest and it is the most obscene and it is the true one. Every ounce of everything I had carried since Doreen Callas's fence went out of me and into that room, and the going-out of it was the purest physical pleasure I have known in my life, and I have never been touched by anybody in a way that came near it.

That is what a relief is. That is the kindness at the end. That is what Adele Storr meant, in perfect sincerity, when she said you're emptied, love, and you've earned it, and what the thirty people in the hall were grateful for, and what Doreen Callas brought me a plant about.
They are not wrong. It is the greatest gift Halloran has to give and it gives it once a decade and it is real.
I came back on the floor.
There is no other way to say it. There was nothing, and then there was a room, and I was on my knees in it with my hands on the boards and the boards were wet.
The first thing I was aware of, before anything else, before her, was my hands.
They were open.

I knelt there and I opened and closed my right hand four or five times and it went all the way, easy, no catch, no hook, the hand of a woman of thirty-seven, and I did that for I do not know how long before I understood what I was kneeling in.
Then I understood what I was kneeling in.
I am not going to describe her. I have described the doing of it and that is what I owed. The result belongs to her and she is not here to permit it.
She was alive.

Her eyes were open and they found me. There was breath going in and out, wrong, wet, but going. She had minutes. She had kept them; I believe that absolutely, I believe that woman held on to the last of herself for that quarter of an hour by an act of will that I am not fit to describe.
And she began to talk.
She started with the year. 1889. She had a date and she said the date.

She said a number of families. She said what they had been doing there in the spring of that year and what the arrangement had been, and she said the name of a man who had signed something, and she said the name of the thing he had signed, and she said what was in the fourth clause of it and what had happened in the November after.

She said where the line had actually run — the true line, the one in the original, which is why the road goes round, which is why the markers have been wrong since her father's time, which is why somebody in 1912 planted a row of poplars along a boundary that no longer legally existed and every farmer in Halloran has wanted to take a chainsaw to it ever since without knowing why.
She said what happened at the east end of the field in the winter of 1889 and how many, and she said it flatly, the way a woman gives an account to a clerk.
And then she said the name.

She said what the land was called. The whole name, the way it was said, and then she said it again more slowly because the first time it had come out wrong through the blood, and she looked at me while she said it and she waited.
And I knelt there with my beautiful working hands and no pen.
There was no pen in that cottage. There was no book.

You go to a crossing with nothing. That is the custom, that is what everybody knows, they take your coat in the hall and you walk out with empty pockets and empty hands, and it is done for the kindest of reasons — Adele has said it to me herself — because a person at the end of the walk should not have to be encumbered with anything.
Don't go out at dusk with nothing in your pockets.

Nine years he had, and one page, and he spent it on a woman he had loved, and he gave me the whole of the rest of it in the door of a hotel bar in eleven words and I did not understand a single one of them until I was kneeling on the floor with the answer coming out of a dying woman's mouth and nothing in my hands to catch it with.
What is spoken is only weather.

I knew it. I had known it since my first evening in that town, over tea, with the radiator on too high — Adele told me and she told me straight and she never once told me a lie. It doesn't work if someone else writes it. It doesn't work if you record it and write it up after. The hand has to be yours and it has to be at the time.

There was no time. That is the thing. Even if I had run — and I did think of running, I thought of it in the middle of her saying the fourth clause, I thought of the Office and the desk and the ledger eleven hundred yards away up the field road — she had perhaps four minutes left and it is a twelve-minute walk and she could not have said it twice.

Forty years she spent making herself unloved. Forty years of being cold at funerals and standing apart at the fete and never joining anything, deliberately, patiently, so that four thousand people would file her down to the bottom of the sheet and the water would run to her. She built the door and she got herself put behind it and she was right about every part of it except the smallest one, which is that a Taker walks to her crossing with empty pockets because the town is being considerate.

She got to the end of it. I made her get to the end of it — I said go on, I said the fourth clause again, I said the name, say the name again — and she said it all, twice, into a room with no scribe in it.
And then she stopped, and looked at me for a while longer, and I watched her work out what had happened.
She did not look angry. I have wished for three years that she had looked angry.
She looked tired. That is all. She looked like a woman who has carried two bags of shopping a very long way and has arrived at the door and found she has the wrong key, and is too tired to go back.
She died about four minutes after that, still looking at me, and she took it with her.
I searched that house until the light came.

Every drawer. Behind the plates. Under the mattress and inside it, I opened the mattress. The floorboards in the back room, three of which came up and none of which had anything under them but dust and a marble. The cold hearth, which I went through with my hands to the bottom and which had nothing in it but forty years of ash and a nail.
There was a Bible with nothing written in it. There was a photograph album with the photographs unlabelled. There was a shoebox of receipts.

She had written nothing down. Not one word, not one name, not a date, not a mark. And I understood why before I had finished looking — because anything written can be found, and a thing found in Halloran goes into the ARCHIVE drawer in the grey cabinet behind the door where the key hangs on a nail, and is indexed, and is consolidated onto a single sheet, and the cards are burned.

The only safe place in that town was inside a person, and the only person who could hold anything was the one they emptied once a decade, and she had worked all of that out, correctly, from first principles, over four decades, alone.
She was the cleverest human being I have ever met and she was wrong by one detail and the detail was a courtesy about pockets.

The land's first name went out of the world in a front room on the field road at about ten past nine on the eleventh of May, and it went as thoroughly as the men with the theodolite could ever have wished, and it was not taken from her. It was not suppressed. Nobody silenced her.
It was mislaid. By procedure. By a filing convention and a small kindness about coats.
They gave me the second cottage from the end.

It is a good house. I want to say that without any irony at all, because it is true and because everything in this account has been true. It is warm, and it is dry, and the Office keeps it, and there is a garden with a wall.
The town has been wonderful to me.

That is not a figure of speech. Doreen Callas came twice a week until she died last year. The women from the church do my shopping on a rota that is oversubscribed. Children are sent down the field road with cake and they are pleased to be sent. Adele comes on Sundays and sits in the good chair and tells me about her son, who is doing well now, and about the fete, and about her sister-in-law, and she has never once, in three years, said anything to me that was not kind.
They loved Cortland Freem too. They took him casseroles for eleven years before he died at the north end of town and never once thought about who he had been in the ledger.

I have understood, latterly, what the love is. It is not gratitude, although everyone doing it would tell you it is gratitude. It is what you feel for someone you have got away with something in front of. It is enormous, and it is warm, and it is completely genuine, and it is the exact size of what they handed over.
The hands never went back. That is the thing nobody prepared me for and it is the sentence I have been serving.

I was told, and I believed, that Takers are ruined by the work. They are not. They are ruined by the load, and when the load comes off, the body comes back. My hands are perfect. I am forty and I could scrub a floor. Ottmar Lisk sat in a chair with a blanket over his knees for fourteen months with hands that would not hold a cup, and I thought that was the office, and it was not the office. It was that they had emptied him into a man called Cortland Freem and there was not enough left of Ottmar Lisk afterward to notice that his hands had come back.

There was enough left of me. That is my whole misfortune and I do not know why it fell out that way. Perhaps three years is not long enough to wear a person all the way through. Perhaps it is because I went in with something of my own and it was still there when everything else went, so that when the load came off there was one thing still standing in the middle of the empty room, and it was me, and it was my mother's face, and it was the whole of my remaining furniture.
So I have had three years of perfect health in a good small house, being loved, in which to be nothing but guilty.
Adele brought me the ledger this morning.

She brought it on a Sunday, in a canvas bag, with a pen, because that is the custom and it is called the kindness at the end. She put it on the table by the window where the light is and she said, "There's no hurry. Ottmar took a year over his."

She has been coming for three years and she has never once asked me what happened in that room. It has not occurred to her that anything happened in that room. A relief happened, and an old woman at the field end of town had a fall at home, and the two things sit in Adele Storr's head eleven inches apart and have never touched, and the reason they have never touched is that I write down everything that might make them touch, four times a year, in longhand, for thirty years before I came and for ninety years before that.

There is a new one, by the way. She came in the spring, off the same bus, at the same crossroads. She is a widow of about forty from three counties over and she has no family and a clean hand and, I would guess, a great deal of experience of not saying things. Adele says she is settling in wonderfully. Adele says she is filling nicely.

She will read the back pages on her first night. It is required; it is the induction; she will sit on the bed above the wool shop with ten pages in her lap and read every Taker's last entry going back to 1911, and mine will be the newest and the clearest and the easiest to read, because I am the only one of us whose hand came back.
So I have thought very hard about what to put on it.

I know the mechanism. I know about the cup and the wall and the hand. I know that the Office does not choose, that it only counts, that the sheet is a weather map and Adele files it without reading it. I know that there was a fourth clause and a November in 1889 and a line that ran somewhere else. I do not know the name — that went into the floor of a front room on the eleventh of

May — but I know that there was one, and that there is a woman under a stone in the churchyard who spent eighty-four years being disliked on purpose so that somebody would find out, and that the whole of what she got for it was me.
I could write all of that. There is room. My hand is fine.
And I have been sitting here since Adele went, with the pen, in the light, and what I have found is that I do not want to.
I want to put down my mother.

That is the truth of it and it is the last true thing I have. I have had three years in this house with nothing in me but nine years of a woman who hated me for being kind to her, and it is mine, it has always been mine, nobody ever took it, and there is a book on this table that takes things and there is a pen beside it and I am so tired.

They will give it to a widow of about forty who is settling in wonderfully. She will read it and she will feel for me, because she is porous, that is why they hired her, and it will go into her the way the fence went into me, and she will carry it, and in eight or nine years she will be walked out at dusk with empty pockets and it will go out of her into whoever the counting finds.
And I will be light.

That is what this town does. It has one thing to offer and it has offered it to everybody, for ninety years, honestly, in writing, and it works, and I have watched what it costs and I know exactly what I am doing and I am going to do it anyway, because I am tired, and because it is the only thing anybody has ever given me.
My mother was ill for nine years and I nursed her, and there was no one else, and she hated me for it.
There. It is down. It took no time at all.

I am going to sit here a while and then I will put the pen in the bag with the book, and Adele will collect it next Sunday and file it, and in the spring a woman I have not met will read it on a bed above the wool shop and find nothing in it but a daughter and a mother and the ordinary bitterness of a life, in a hand she will assume belonged to somebody who simply grew old in the work.
She will not read anything else, because there is nothing else in the book.
Then she will go down to the Office, and Adele will be delighted to see her, and there will be tea.
Then she will take the cup.
